newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Deutz aims for operating breakeven.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Deutz aims for operating breakeven.

text.p: Deutz AG, the German motor maker risen from the wreckage of Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG, said Tuesday it returned to net profit in 1996 after a bailout, and its operations would break even this year.

Chairman Anton Schneider told a news conference the company made a net profit of 874 German million marks ($506 million) in 1996, after a net loss of 1.134 billion marks ($657 million) the year before. The profit resulted entirely from 897 million marks ($519 million) in one-time gains, mainly banks' contributions to last year's rescue.

Schneider said the company posted an operating loss of 56 million marks ($32.4 million) in 1996, but there would be no losses in 1997, and 1998 would show further improvement as it continued to restructure, shedding subsidiaries and focusing solely on motors.
"Our strategy is very clear: motors, motors, motors," Schneider said of Deutz, which makes a wide range of motors for construction equipment, pumps and compressors as well as cars, trucks and buses.

Deutz is now holding talks with potential buyers for its environmental technology and Indumont units, and hopes to sell them by June 30. Indumont builds, services and maintains industrial plants, particularly in pipeline and conveyor systems. The company aims to sell its cement technology and raw materials processing activities by the end of the year.

It also still plans to sell its KHD Humboldt Wedag unit, whose contracts for three Saudi cement plants were the source of the original losses that led to the $1 billion-mark ($579 million) bailout by the company's creditor banks led by Deutsche Bank AG.
One of the three plants has been completed and delivered. A second is to be finished by June 30, and the third by the end of October.
